task_row_model.query: How can I recursively reverse a singly linked list in place in Python? Explain the base case, the pointer reassignment steps, and the time and space complexity.

documents.content: An iterative approach to reverse a singly linked list walks through the list and reassigns pointers in one pass. Initialize three pointers: prev = None, current = head, next_node = None. While current is not None, set next_node = current.next, current.next = prev, then prev = current and current = next_node. After the loop prev becomes the new head. This method runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. It is straightforward, avoids recursion, and is commonly used in production code where recursion depth might be a concern.
documents.reasoning_trace: Recognized as relevant because it describes pointer reassignment to reverse a singly linked list in place. However, it explains the iterative algorithm, not the recursive version requested, so it only partially answers the query.

documents.content: To reverse a singly linked list recursively, use the base case: if head is None or head.next is None return head. For the recursive step call new_head = reverse(head.next). After that, rewire pointers so that head.next.next = head and head.next = None; finally return new_head. This works because reverse(head.next) returns the head of the reversed sublist, and setting head.next.next points the last node of that sublist back to head. Time complexity is O(n) since each node is visited once; space complexity is O(n) due to recursion call stack in typical languages like Python.
documents.reasoning_trace: Matched all query requirements: identifies correct base case, gives exact pointer reassignment (head.next.next = head, head.next = None), explains why it works, and states time O(n) and space O(n) due to recursion. Therefore this document fully answers the question.

documents.content: An alternative is to convert a singly linked list to an array, reverse the array, and rebuild the list. Traverse the list to collect node values in a list, reverse that list of values, then create a new linked list nodes in that order. This technique is easy to implement and useful when node objects are immutable or when you need random access during reversal. It takes O(n) time for traversal and O(n) extra space for the array and rebuilt nodes. Note that this does not reverse the original links in place; it constructs a new list.

documents.content: Cycle detection in a singly linked list can be done with Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm. Use two pointers, slow and fast, both starting at head. In each step advance slow by one and fast by two nodes. If they meet, a cycle exists. To find the cycle start, reset one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time until they meet again; that node is the cycle entry. This algorithm uses O(n) time and O(1) space and is efficient for detecting loops in link structures.

documents.content: To reverse a doubly linked list in place, walk the list and swap the next and prev pointers for each node. Start at the current head and for each node do temp = node.next, node.next = node.prev, node.prev = temp, then move to node.prev (which is the original next). At the end update the head to be the last processed node. This procedure exploits the prev pointer to reverse direction efficiently and runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space. It relies on having both next and prev fields available.
